lesson.title: Reversing the Tangent Rule: The Integral of sec^2(x)
lesson.summary: Since tan(x) differentiates to sec^2(x), integrating sec^2(x) hands you tan(x) back, one of the most frequently used rules in the trig integral family.
lesson.body:
The integral of sec^2(x) is: integral of sec^2(x) dx = tan(x) + C.

This rule is the derivative of tangent read backward. You already know that the derivative of tan(x) is sec^2(x). Since differentiating tan(x) produces sec^2(x), by the definition of an antiderivative, tan(x) is an antiderivative of sec^2(x). No extra algebra is required, the integral rule is simply the derivative fact viewed in reverse, the same reverse engineering approach introduced for the whole basic trig integral family.

One practical note on domain: tan(x) and sec^2(x) are both undefined wherever cos(x) = 0, at odd multiples of pi/2. The antiderivative rule holds on any interval that avoids those points, since that is also exactly where sec^2(x) itself is undefined, so there is no new restriction being introduced by integrating.

Worked example: find integral of 7*sec^2(x) dx. Apply the constant multiple rule first: 7 * integral of sec^2(x) dx = 7*tan(x) + C. Verify by differentiating: the derivative of 7*tan(x) is 7*sec^2(x), which matches the original integrand.

This particular rule shows up constantly once you start solving more complicated integration problems, because sec^2(x) appears naturally whenever tangent functions are involved in a problem, whether directly or after some algebraic rearrangement. Having integral of sec^2(x) dx = tan(x) + C ready to use without hesitation is one of the more valuable pieces of fluency you can build in this unit.
